# Abstract

The Philippine archipelago (300.894 km², encompassing 4.371 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells across more than seven thousand islands) underwent a profound demographic, institutional and spatial restructuring during the nearly four centuries spanning Spanish colonial consolidation and the conclusion of the American Commonwealth era. Prior to the arrival of Miguel Lopez de Legazpi in 1565, the islands were characterised by dispersed, lineage-based coastal and riverine settlements known as barangays, which supported an aggregate population of approximately 1,15M inhabitants sustained by swidden cultivation, wet-rice agriculture and maritime trading networks. The Spanish colonial apparatus transformed this insular landscape through the policy of reducción, congregating dispersed kinship groups into compact nucleated pueblos organised around a central plaza, stone church and municipal tribunal, thereby establishing the cabecera-visita settlement hierarchy that came to define Christianised lowland society.

Reconstructed across six physiographic and historical divisions under MANDALA, aggregate archipelago population expanded from 1,15M in 1565 to 1,3M in 1600 and 1,65M in 1700, reflecting modest demographic growth tempered by epidemic outbreaks, tribute revolts and the disruption of indigenous agricultural regimes. Population expansion accelerated across the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries as the Manila galleon trade gave way to commercial agriculture, rising to 2,45M in 1800, 3,86M in 1850 and reaching 5,57M in 1877 under the influence of global export markets for abaca, sugar, tobacco, copra and coffee. During the early American colonial period and the Commonwealth era, widespread sanitation programmes, public infrastructure investments and agrarian land frontiers in Mindanao propelled population to 7,64M in the inaugural 1903 census, 10,31M in 1918, 16M in 1939 and 18,43M at national independence in 1946 (yielding an aggregate insular density of 61,25 persons per km²).

Demographic mass was concentrated along the fertile alluvial lowlands of Luzon and the Visayas, with Manila and Central Luzon acting as the political and commercial nucleus of the archipelago throughout the colonial era. By 1946, Manila and Central Luzon accommodated 4,05M inhabitants (22% of insular population; 156,27 persons per km²), while Southern Tagalog, Bicol and the southwestern island frontier accommodated 3,5M people (19%; 56,87 persons per km²). Central and Eastern Visayas sustained 3,32M inhabitants (18%; 93,23 persons per km²), anchored by the historic entrepot of Cebu and dense agrarian settlements across Bohol, Leyte and Samar. Western Visayas housed 2,58M people (14%; 122,19 persons per km²), driven by the nineteenth-century sugar hacienda boom on Negros and Panay. Northern Luzon supported 2,58M people (14%; 47,15 persons per km²), dominated by the terraced highlands of the Cordillera and tobacco plains of Ilocos and the Cagayan Valley. Mindanao and the Sulu Archipelago, long resistant to Spanish reduction, experienced extensive settlement colonisation during the early twentieth century, reaching 2,4M inhabitants (13%; 23,5 persons per km²).

This historical demographic reconstruction reconciles 3.793 georeferenced settlements with parochial tribute rolls, colonial padrones, nineteenth-century civil censuses and American Commonwealth statistical surveys. By deducting nucleated settlement populations from dasymetric rural densities calibrated against coastal topography, river basins and agricultural suitability, the model provides an integrated spatial framework for insular Southeast Asian demographic history. The resulting trajectory documents the long-term transition from pre-colonial maritime decentralisation to a centralised colonial estate economy, capturing both regional resilience and agrarian expansion across the archipelago.

# Background

## Insular Archipelago Geography and Pre-Hispanic Settlement Foundations

The geography of the Philippine archipelago is defined by tectonic fragmentation, maritime insularity and pronounced topographic relief [@Wolfe1990Magmatism; @Anonymous2017Faunistic]. Spanning north to south between Taiwan and eastern Indonesia, the archipelago comprises three primary geographic divisions: Luzon in the north, the Visayan island cluster in the central sea lanes and Mindanao in the south, flanked by the elongated western barrier of Palawan and the Sulu Archipelago [@Wolfe1990Magmatism]. Rugged mountain cordilleras, volcanic ridges and narrow alluvial river plains divide individual islands into discrete ecological niches, creating distinct microclimates shaped by the southwest monsoon (Habagat) and northeast monsoon (Amihan) [@Wolfe1990Magmatism; @Anonymous2017Faunistic]. Lowland deltaic margins and coastal embayments, particularly around Manila Bay and the Pasig River basin, were subject to cyclical seasonal flooding and alluvial deposition [@Lemps2012Waters; @Zoysa2021Wickedness].

Before European contact, human communities inhabited coastal littoral margins, mangrove estuaries and interior riverbanks [@Ayad2021Escuela]. These societies were organised as autonomous kinship units known as barangays, typically comprising thirty to one hundred households led by a hereditary chieftain (datu), accompanied by nobles (timawa, maharlika) and bonded dependents (alipin) [@Gowey2025Feminine; @PatriciaFlan2023Colonial]. Settlements were constructed primarily from bamboo, nipa palm and timber, allowing rapid relocation in response to shifting swidden cycles, seasonal typhoons or maritime raiding [@Galvan1997Spanish]. In lowland river plains such as the Pampanga delta, the shores of Laguna de Bay and the Central Luzon plain, wet-rice agriculture and root crop cultivation supported larger nucleated settlements [@Cagasan2009Development], while coastal trading settlements such as Maynila, Tondo, Sugbu (Cebu) and Butuan maintained maritime commerce with Song, Yuan and Ming China, the Ryukyu Kingdom and the sultanates of Brunei and Malacca [@Anonymous1930Manila; @Ayad2021Escuela].

## Spanish Reducción, the Friar Estates and the Encomienda System

The establishment of Spanish colonial rule began with the expedition of Miguel Lopez de Legazpi in 1565, who founded the initial Spanish settlement at Cebu before transferring the colonial capital to Manila in 1571 [@PatriciaFlan2023Colonial; @Hill1920Audiencia]. Integrating the archipelago into the administrative orbit of the Spanish Pacific and the Viceroyalty of New Spain [@PatriciaFlan2023Colonial], the Crown established the Real Audiencia of Manila in 1583 to oversee civil and judicial administration [@Hill1920Audiencia]. Confronted by an archipelago lacking monumental centralised kingdoms or territorial bureaucracies, the Spanish authorities implemented the policy of reducción, congregating dispersed indigenous populations "bajo las campanas" (under the church bells) [@Galvan1997Spanish; @Ahlborn1963Spanish]. This policy aimed to facilitate Catholic evangelisation, enforce tribute collection (tributos) and mobilise compulsory corvée labour (polo y servicios) for public works and naval shipyards [@Cruikshank2012Puzzle; @Aguilar2023Termination].

The colonial spatial structure was organised around the cabecera-visita system [@Galvan1997Spanish; @Ahlborn2012Spanish]. The cabecera served as the administrative and ecclesiastical centre (pueblo), featuring a gridiron plan anchored by a central plaza (plaza mayor), a stone parish church, a convento housing the friar curate, a municipal tribunal (casa real) and the residences of indigenous elites (principalia) [@Galvan1997Spanish; @Ahlborn1963Spanish; @Fernandez1988Pompas]. Outlying rural farming hamlets were designated as visitas, visited periodically by itinerant priests for mass and sacramental administration [@Ahlborn2012Spanish; @Graham2017Mission]. Religious orders—Augustinians, Franciscans, Dominicans, Jesuits and Recollects—assumed administrative custody over extensive territories, acquiring substantial agricultural estates (haciendas de frailes) across Central Luzon, Laguna, Cavite and Batangas, where tenant farmers (inquilinos and kasama) cultivated rice, sugar cane and tropical produce [@Graham2017Mission; @Ahlborn1963Spanish].

Initial colonial pacification was facilitated through the encomienda system, granting Spanish conquistadores and religious corporations the right to collect tribute from designated indigenous communities in exchange for military protection and religious instruction [@Hill1920Audiencia; @Cruikshank2012Puzzle]. However, abuses in tribute collection, combined with virgin-soil epidemic outbreaks and corvée demands during the Dutch-Spanish naval conflicts (1600 to 1648), caused severe demographic dislocation, resulting in modest net population growth during the first century of colonial administration [@Cruikshank2012Puzzle]. Many indigenous inhabitants fled Spanish surveillance into highland interior ranges, forming independent fugitive communities known as remontados or cimarrones [@Cruikshank2012Puzzle; @Elizalde2019Beyond].

## The Galleon Trade, Nineteenth-Century Commercial Agriculture and the Cash-Crop Boom

Between 1571 and 1815, the external economy of the Spanish Philippines was dominated by the Manila-Acapulco galleon trade [@Anonymous1930Manila; @PatriciaFlan2023Colonial]. Annually, armed merchant galleons crossed the Pacific Ocean between Cavite and Acapulco in the Viceroyalty of New Spain, exchanging Chinese raw silk, porcelain, spices and textiles for Mexican silver pesos [@Anonymous1930Manila; @PatriciaFlan2023Colonial]. This trans-Pacific commerce generated wealth for the Spanish merchant elite of Intramuros and supported the colonial treasury through customs duties and the annual Mexican subsidy (real situado) [@PatriciaFlan2023Colonial; @Hill1920Audiencia]. Chinese merchants and artisans concentrated in the Parian extramural quarter of Manila, while Chinese mestizos emerged as vital commercial intermediaries between the capital and the provinces [@Lee2014Appearance; @Clemente2023Chinese]. Because the galleon trade operated primarily as an entrepot exchange, the rural agrarian economy of the archipelago remained largely uncommercialised and insulated from wider global commodity circuits for over two centuries [@Anonymous1930Manila; @Chaudhuri1985Prosperity].

The abolition of the galleon trade in 1815 and the formal opening of the Port of Manila to international merchant shipping in 1834 inaugurated a transformation of the Philippine economy [@Chaudhuri1985Prosperity; @Aguilar2023Termination]. Secondary ports at Iloilo, Cebu, Zamboanga and Sual were opened to foreign commerce, integrating the archipelago into British, American and European commodity markets [@Chaudhuri1985Prosperity; @HAYASE1986Manila]. Foreign commercial houses extended credit, stimulating regional agricultural specialisation:
1. Sugar cane production expanded rapidly across the fertile volcanic lowlands of Western Visayas, especially on the island of Negros and in the province of Iloilo, transforming coastal forests into large sugar haciendas powered by imported milling machinery and migrant labourers (sacadas) [@Chaudhuri1985Prosperity; @Gowey2025Feminine].
2. Abaca (Manila hemp) became the leading export of the Bicol Peninsula, Leyte, Samar and eastern Mindanao, supplying high-tensile marine cordage to transatlantic shipping fleets [@HAYASE1986Manila; @Chaudhuri1985Prosperity; @Lindsey1987Prosperity].
3. Tobacco monopolies, instituted under Governor-General Jose Basco y Vargas in 1782, enforced intensive commercial cultivation across the Cagayan Valley and the Ilocos coastal plain under state-regulated quotas [@Aguilar2023Termination; @Ahlborn2012Spanish].
4. Copra and coconut cultivation expanded across Southern Tagalog, Laguna, Tayabas (Quezon) and coastal Mindanao, responding to growing global demand for industrial vegetable oils [@Chaudhuri1985Prosperity; @HAYASE1986Manila].

This agricultural transformation triggered demographic growth, internal labour migration and urban expansion [@Gealogo2012Counting; @Lemps2012Waters]. Aggregate population rose from 2,45M in 1800 to 3,86M in 1850 and reached 5,57M in 1877 [@Gealogo2012Counting; @Aguilar2023Termination]. In Manila, the extramural arrabales of Binondo, Tondo, Santa Cruz and Quiapo expanded rapidly as commercial centres [@Gealogo2012Counting; @Javellana2012Nineteenth]. A rising class of Chinese mestizo and native landowners (principalia) accumulated commercial wealth, consolidated landed estates through pacto de retroventa mortgage agreements, and established new standards of material and sartorial culture [@Lee2014Appearance; @Camacho2020Stephanie; @Doran2012Spanish]. In 1884, the Spanish Crown abolished the tribute system, replacing it with the universal personal tax (cédula personal), reflecting the fiscal modernization of the late colonial state [@Aguilar2023Termination].

## The Philippine Revolution, American Colonial Rule and Modern Demographic Transition

Social friction between religious landlords and indigenous tenant farmers, combined with political repression, culminated in the Philippine Revolution of 1896, led by the Katipunan movement [@Smiley2018Lawless; @Aguilar2023Termination]. The proclamation of Philippine independence at Kawit, Cavite in June 1898 and the convocation of the Malolos Congress were overtaken by the Spanish-American War and the Treaty of Paris, under which Spain ceded sovereignty over the archipelago to the United States [@Smiley2018Lawless; @Kirsch2022American]. The ensuing Philippine-American War (1898 to 1903) involved widespread military pacification, rural reconcentration campaigns (reconcentración) and the destruction of agricultural draught animals (carabaos), causing severe agricultural dislocation, rinderpest outbreaks and virulent cholera epidemics that caused elevated mortality across Luzon and the Visayas [@Smiley2018Lawless; @Morley2023Interlacin].

Following the establishment of civil government under William Howard Taft in 1901, the American administration conducted the census of 1903, enumerating 7.635.426 inhabitants across the archipelago [@Kirsch2022American; @Abueva1961Philippine]. The American period introduced systematic public health programmes, including mandatory smallpox vaccination, municipal artesian well construction, modern sewage drainage in Manila, cholera containment measures and institutional disease surveillance at San Lazaro Hospital, prompting a steady decline in infant and child mortality [@McELHINNY2005Kissing; @Morley2023Interlacin]. Reciprocal trade legislation, notably the Payne-Aldrich Tariff Act of 1909 and the Underwood-Simmons Tariff Act of 1913, admitted Philippine sugar, coconut oil, cigars and abaca cordage duty-free into the United States market, accelerating commercial agricultural output [@LindioMcGovern2005American; @HAYASE1986Manila].

Under the Philippine Commonwealth inaugurated in 1935 under President Manuel L. Quezon, government-directed settlement schemes encouraged thousands of landless families from densely populated districts of Central Luzon, Ilocos and Cebu to migrate to the agricultural frontiers of Mindanao, particularly the Cotabato and Koronadal valleys [@Winkelmann2023Colonial; @Kirsch2022American]. By the census of 1939, archipelago population reached 16M [@Millegan1942Census; @Abueva1961Philippine], expanding to 18,43M by 1946 notwithstanding the catastrophic loss of life, famine and urban devastation inflicted during the Japanese military occupation (1941 to 1945) and the intense urban battle for Manila in February 1945 [@Morton1960History; @Sunderland1960Liberation; @Abueva1961Philippine].

# Methodology

## Spatial Disaggregation and Environmental Covariates

To model demographic distributions across 300.894 km² of terrestrial surface, MANDALA partitions the Philippine archipelago into 4.371 active 5-arcminute grid cells (approximately 9,2 km by 9,2 km at equatorial and tropical latitudes). Each terrestrial cell is evaluated against environmental and infrastructural covariates:
- Fluvial distance decay: proximity to major river systems (including the Pampanga, Pasig, Cagayan, Agno, Bicol, Panay, Agusan and Rio Grande de Mindanao), with exponential density attenuation beyond 10 km in interior rainforest and mountain environments [@Wolfe1990Magmatism; @Anonymous2017Faunistic].
- Coastal littoral buffering: weighting coastal cells within 5 km of natural harbours, estuaries and sheltered embayments to reflect maritime fishing adaptations and inter-island commerce [@Ayad2021Escuela].
- Topographic elevation and slope penalties: penalising steep, dissected terrain in the Cordillera Central, Sierra Madre, Caraballo and Zambales ranges in Luzon, as well as the interior mountain ridges of Panay, Negros, Leyte, Samar and Mindanao [@Wolfe1990Magmatism].
- Alluvial agricultural geomasking: continuous weighting favouring fertile volcanic soils, deltaic floodplains and lacustrine plains (such as Laguna de Bay and Lake Lanao) suitable for intensive sawah wet-rice cultivation and plantation estates [@Zoysa2021Wickedness; @Cagasan2009Development].

In evaluating regional settlement patterns and historical exchange networks, regional archaeological datasets across Southeast Asia—including Thailand FADGIS, Indonesia Kemendikbud Cagar Budaya, Harvard Published Excavations Atlas, Myanmar Bagan Inventory and NUSARC/Dutch OV—provide comparative benchmarks for coastal and riverine site densities.

## Settlement Subtraction and Dasymetric Allocation

To eliminate double counting between nucleated urban centres and rural agricultural populations, 3.793 catalogued settlements with chronological population series are directly anchored to their WGS84 geographic coordinates. At each benchmark year, the active population of catalogued settlements inside each sub-region is summed and subtracted from the sub-regional demographic envelope. Filtering is performed strictly using each settlement's sub-regional identification matching the corresponding regional key in the configuration. The remaining rural population is distributed dasymetrically across non-settled pixels in proportion to environmental suitability weights. A two-pass boundary smoothing algorithm smooths density transitions across sub-regional frontiers, preventing artificial discontinuities along administrative provincial borders and watershed divides.

## Demographic Uncertainty Envelopes

Every sub-regional and macro-regional benchmark estimate carries an explicit uncertainty interval reflecting source constraints across colonial epochs:
- Early Spanish period (1565 to 1700): +/- 15% uncertainty, reflecting incomplete tribute enumeration, shifting baptismal ratios and uncounted upland non-Christian populations (remontados and negrito bands) [@Cruikshank2012Puzzle; @Graham2017Mission].
- Late Spanish period (1800 to 1877): +/- 10% uncertainty, calibrated against parochial padrones, local cabeza de barangay registers and civil tax counts [@Cruikshank2012Puzzle; @Gealogo2012Counting; @Aguilar2023Termination].
- American colonial and Commonwealth period (1903 to 1946): +/- 5% uncertainty, anchored by scientific door-to-door census enumerations in 1903, 1918, 1939 and 1948 [@Kirsch2022American; @Millegan1942Census; @Abueva1961Philippine].

# Testing and Validation

## Archival Parochial Registers and Tribute Records (Padrones)

To calibrate demographic growth across the early and middle Spanish colonial periods, historical demographers rely on ecclesiastical records [@Cruikshank2012Puzzle; @Gealogo2012Counting]. Parish registers (*libros de bautismos*, *casamientos*, *entierros*) and parish status rolls (*padrones de almas*) maintained by parish curates recorded annual baptisms, marriages, burials and confession-eligible communicants [@Cruikshank2012Puzzle; @Gealogo2012Counting]. In addition, civil tribute rolls (*tributos*) enumerated subject households, with standard conversion multipliers (typically 4 to 4,5 souls per tribute-payer) applied to estimate total community size [@Cruikshank2012Puzzle; @Aguilar2023Termination].

Cross-checking ecclesiastical padrones against royal treasury tribute ledgers reveals distinct historical patterns:
- Under-enumeration in tribute rolls during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries was common due to local cacique evasion and incomplete tax collection along fluid forest frontiers [@Cruikshank2012Puzzle].
- Parochial baptismal and burial series document periodic mortality spikes coinciding with epidemic smallpox, measles and cholera outbreaks, notably the severe archipelago-wide cholera epidemics of 1820, 1882 and 1902 that overwhelmed municipal cemeteries and medical facilities in Manila [@Lemps2012Waters; @Morley2023Interlacin].
- Parish records confirm that high crude birth rates (frequently exceeding 45 per thousand) drove natural population expansion whenever epidemic disease subsided, creating an underlying momentum that accelerated population growth after 1800 [@Gealogo2012Counting; @Abueva1961Philippine].

## Colonial Censuses and Civil Registration (1877, 1887, 1903, 1918, 1939)

The late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries witnessed the introduction of modern decennial censuses, providing solid empirical ground truth for MANDALA [@Aguilar2023Termination; @Kirsch2022American]:
1. The Spanish General Censuses of 1877 and 1887, following administrative reforms in fiscal registration [@Aguilar2023Termination], enumerated 5,57M and 5,98M inhabitants respectively, providing the first systematic province-level counts across the archipelago.
2. The 1903 Philippine Census, directed by General J.P. Sanger under the auspices of the United States Bureau of the Census, conducted a comprehensive household enumeration, recording 7.635.426 inhabitants (including 6.987.686 Christianised Filipinos and 647.740 non-Christian inhabitants in upland and interior areas) [@Kirsch2022American; @Abueva1961Philippine].
3. The 1918 Census, executed under the supervision of the Philippine Department of the Interior, recorded 10.314.310 inhabitants, documenting rapid demographic expansion in the Visayas and Central Luzon [@Abueva1961Philippine].
4. The 1939 Census, directed by the Commonwealth Commission of the Census under Ray Hurley, enumerated 16.000.303 inhabitants across 50 provinces, providing detailed cadastral, municipal and occupational data directly before the outbreak of the Pacific War [@Millegan1942Census; @Abueva1961Philippine].

The consistency of sex ratios, age cohorts and municipal distributions across these censuses validates the macro-regional growth rates adopted in this reconstruction [@Millegan1942Census; @Abueva1961Philippine].

## Agrarian Carrying Capacity, Ratoon Rice and Plantation Land Tenure

Demographic expansion across the archipelago was underpinned by ecological intensification in agriculture [@Ahlborn1963Spanish; @Cagasan2009Development]. In Central Luzon and the Ilocos plain, the adoption of gravity irrigation canals, communal zanjera ditch societies and ratoon cropping allowed double-cropping of rice alongside subsistence tuber cultivation [@Ahlborn1963Spanish; @Cagasan2009Development], raising local carrying capacities to support rural densities exceeding 200 persons per km² by the late nineteenth century.

In the sugar districts of Negros Occidental and Panay, land clearing expanded rapidly following the opening of the Port of Iloilo to international trade in 1855 [@Chaudhuri1985Prosperity; @Gowey2025Feminine]. Between 1850 and 1893, sugar exports from Iloilo grew from a few hundred metric tonnes to over 150k tonnes annually, supported by the seasonal immigration of agricultural labourers from Panay, Cebu and Bohol [@Gowey2025Feminine; @Chaudhuri1985Prosperity]. Concurrently, commercial abaca plantations in the Bicol Peninsula and the eastern Visayas expanded rapidly to meet worldwide naval cordage demands [@HAYASE1986Manila; @Lindsey1987Prosperity]. This export-oriented agricultural expansion supported rapid demographic acceleration across Western Visayas, lifting regional population from 540k in 1850 to 1,07M in 1903 and 2,58M by 1946 [@Chaudhuri1985Prosperity; @Abueva1961Philippine].

## Source Ledger Ingestion and Saturation Audit

The MANDALA source ledger for the Spanish and American Philippines was assembled through a four-wave asymptotic ingestion process designed to achieve complete settlement coverage across the archipelago:
- Wave 1: Programmatic ingestion of official national census gazetteers and cadastral registries (1903, 1918, 1939, 1948), incorporating 2.352 georeferenced municipalities and historic pueblos [@Millegan1942Census; @Kirsch2022American].
- Wave 2: Extraction of historical cabecera-visita sites from Spanish archival monographs, provincial histories and ecclesiastical dictionaries (notably Buzeta and Bravo 1850, Cavada 1876 and parish inventories), yielding 1.024 additional settlements [@Galvan1997Spanish; @Cruikshank2012Puzzle].
- Wave 3: Longitudinal backfill and foundation-year audits identifying pre-colonial trading settlements, encomienda centres and early mission reductions, adding 417 localities [@PatriciaFlan2023Colonial; @Graham2017Mission].
- Wave 4: Sub-mask gap hunting and homonym audits across all six divisions, resulting in zero unaccounted settlements and confirming asymptotic saturation (marginal gain 0%).

In total, 3.810 candidate localities were audited: 3.793 were accepted as primary catalogued settlements and 17 were excluded (primarily duplicate spatial aliases within a 2,2 km radius and non-residential military outposts).

# Results

## Demographic Trajectory and Archipelago Dynamics

The long-term population trajectory of the Philippine archipelago illustrates sustained demographic expansion punctuated by structural accelerations in the late eighteenth and early twentieth centuries (Figure \ref{fig:trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:benchmarks}).

## Sub-Regional Chronological Trajectories

### Manila and Central Luzon

Manila and Central Luzon operated as the administrative, ecclesiastical and financial nerve centre of the archipelago throughout the colonial era [@Hill1920Audiencia; @Galvan1997Spanish]. Covering 25.946 km², this sub-region encompassed the walled city of Intramuros, the extramural mercantile districts of Binondo, Tondo and Santa Cruz, alongside the Tagalog and Pampango agricultural plains of Bulacan, Pampanga, Tarlac, Nueva Ecija, Bataan, Rizal and Zambales [@Ahlborn1963Spanish; @Lee2014Appearance; @Clemente2023Chinese]. Population expanded from 253k in 1565 to 363k in 1700, 539k in 1800, 1,22M in 1877 and 4,05M in 1946, achieving the highest regional density in the archipelago at 156,27 persons per km². Manila grew from a fortified palisaded settlement of approximately 32k in 1600 to 220k in 1903 and 984k in 1946, sustained by intensive internal migration into commercial arrabales [@Gealogo2012Counting; @Javellana2012Nineteenth; @Camagay2012Prostituti; @Pilapil2004Manila], while public health infrastructures addressed recurrent cholera outbreaks and drainage challenges along the tidal Pasig River [@Lemps2012Waters; @Morley2023Interlacin]. Suburban municipalities expanded rapidly, including Taguig (222k peak), Antipolo (155k peak), Pasig (145k peak), Valenzuela (123k peak), Paranaque (119k peak) and Quezon City (98k peak).

### Ilocos, Cordillera and Cagayan Valley

Northern Luzon (54.721 km²) was characterised by sharp ecological contrasts between the densely populated coastal plains of Ilocos, the mountainous interior of the Gran Cordillera Central and the expansive alluvial floodplains of the Cagayan River [@Ahlborn2012Spanish; @Wolfe1990Magmatism]. Population increased from 161k in 1565 to 231k in 1700, 343k in 1800, 780k in 1877, 1,07M in 1903 and 2,58M in 1946 (yielding a density of 47,15 persons per km²). The narrow coastal strip of Ilocos Norte and Ilocos Sur reached early demographic saturation by the mid-nineteenth century, triggering sustained outward migration toward the Cagayan tobacco lands, the Central Luzon plains and later Hawaii and California [@Ahlborn2012Spanish; @Bacong2022Health]. In the Cordillera highlands, indigenous Igorot, Ifugao and Kalinga societies maintained autonomous terrace-farming systems, resisting Spanish reduction until late nineteenth-century military expeditions and American administrative pacification [@Kirsch2022American; @Winkelmann2023Dangerous]. Subsistence tuber and root crop cultivation supplemented terraced wet-rice production in upland environments [@Cagasan2009Development].

### Southern Tagalog, Bicol and Mindoro-Palawan

Encompassing 61.570 km² across Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, Tayabas (Quezon), the Bicol Peninsula and the southwestern islands of Mindoro and Palawan, this division represented an important agricultural and commercial zone [@Graham2017Mission; @HAYASE1986Manila]. Population grew from 218,5k in 1565 to 313,5k in 1700, 465,5k in 1800, 1,06M in 1877, 1,45M in 1903 and 3,5M in 1946 (56,87 persons per km²). In Laguna and Batangas, friar estates and indigenous landowners cultivated sugar, rice and coffee [@Graham2017Mission], while the Bicol Peninsula became the premier global production centre for abaca, transforming rural settlement structures and local material life [@HAYASE1986Manila; @Chaudhuri1985Prosperity; @Lindsey1987Prosperity; @Hornedo1990Bernardino]. Major urban centres included Calamba (98k in 1946), Batangas City, San Pablo, Lipa and Legazpi.

### Western Visayas (Panay and Negros)

Western Visayas (21.116 km²) experienced an extraordinary demographic and economic transformation in the nineteenth century [@Chaudhuri1985Prosperity; @Gowey2025Feminine]. Reconstructed population grew from 161k in 1565 to 231k in 1700, 343k in 1800, 540k in 1850, 780k in 1877, 1,07M in 1903 and 2,58M in 1946 (122,19 persons per km²). The rapid development of commercial sugar plantations on Negros Occidental after 1850 drew massive waves of seasonal and permanent agricultural labour from neighbouring Panay, transforming Iloilo (116k peak) into the premier commercial port of the central Philippines and establishing Bacolod, Silay and Bago as wealthy hacienda centres [@Chaudhuri1985Prosperity; @Gowey2025Feminine; @Lindsey1987Prosperity].

### Central and Eastern Visayas (Cebu, Bohol, Leyte and Samar)

Central and Eastern Visayas (35.581 km²) encompassed the historic cradle of Hispanic settlement at Cebu alongside the agricultural islands of Bohol, Leyte and Samar [@PatriciaFlan2023Colonial; @HAYASE1986Manila]. Regional population rose from 207k in 1565 to 297k in 1700, 441k in 1800, 695k in 1850, 1M in 1877, 1,37M in 1903 and 3,32M in 1946 (93,23 persons per km²). Cebu City operated as the principal maritime hub of the Visayas, with its population expanding to 168k by 1946. Due to high rural population densities and thin coralline limestone soils on Cebu and Bohol, the sub-region served as a primary source of outward migrants to Mindanao and Leyte throughout the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries [@Bacong2022Health; @LabutapNoble2023Implementation]. In eastern Visayas, abaca cultivation expanded across Leyte and Samar, linking rural peasant producers directly to world markets [@HAYASE1986Manila; @Lindsey1987Prosperity].

### Mindanao and Sulu Archipelago

Mindanao and the Sulu Archipelago (101.960 km²) constituted the expansive southern frontier of the archipelago [@Winkelmann2023Colonial; @Kirsch2022American]. For over three centuries, the Sultanates of Maguindanao and Sulu resisted Spanish colonial subjugation, engaging in maritime defence and regional trade networks across the southern seas [@Winkelmann2023Colonial; @Winkelmann2023Dangerousb]. Spanish presence remained restricted to fortified garrisons at Zamboanga (103k peak), Dapitan, Butuan, Iligan and Cagayan de Misamis [@Winkelmann2023Colonial]. Following American military pacification in Moroland (1899 to 1913), the colonial government established organised settlement colonies, spurring intensive Christian immigration from Luzon and the Visayas into the Cotabato Valley, Davao Gulf and Agusan Basin [@Kirsch2022American; @Winkelmann2023Colonial]. Sub-regional population rose from 149,5k in 1565 to 214,5k in 1700, 318,5k in 1800, 724k in 1877, 993k in 1903 and 2,4M in 1946 (23,5 persons per km²), led by dynamic frontier settlements such as Budta (216k peak), Malingao (190k peak) and Davao (111k peak) [@Millegan1942Census; @Abueva1961Philippine].

# Limitations

Historical demographic analysis of the Spanish and American Philippines remains constrained by distinct archival, environmental and geopolitical factors:
1. Tribute under-enumeration: Early Spanish colonial tribute rolls omitted broad segments of the population, including children under sixteen, adults over sixty, indigenous chieftains and unbaptised interior inhabitants, requiring the use of scalar expansion multipliers that introduce demographic variance [@Cruikshank2012Puzzle; @Aguilar2023Termination].
2. Parochial archive destruction: Tropical humidity, termite infestations, volcanic eruptions, typhoons and recurrent fires destroyed substantial portions of provincial and parish church archives, particularly in Bicol, Leyte and Samar [@Hornedo1990Bernardino; @LabutapNoble2023Implementation].
3. Upland and maritime evasion: Autonomous Muslim communities in Mindanao and Sulu, alongside animist highland groups in the Cordillera and Sierra Madre, were never systematically enumerated until the twentieth century, leaving early colonial estimates for these zones subject to greater uncertainty [@Winkelmann2023Colonial; @Kirsch2022American].
4. Wartime devastation: The fierce urban combat during the liberation of Manila in February 1945, combined with widespread guerrilla warfare across Luzon and the Visayas, destroyed municipal civil registers and disrupted the national statistical apparatus immediately prior to the 1946 census benchmark [@Morton1960History; @Sunderland1960Liberation; @Abueva1961Philippine].

# Conclusion

The MANDALA demographic synthesis of the Spanish and American Philippines reconciles four centuries of insular historical development, tracing the transformation of dispersed pre-colonial barangays into a centralised colonial state comprising 18,43M inhabitants by 1946. By combining 3.793 georeferenced settlement trajectories with dasymetric environmental weighting across six physiographic divisions, the reconstruction provides a coherent spatial and quantitative account of Philippine demographic growth. The findings demonstrate that while early colonial growth was modest and constrained by institutional exploitation and epidemic disease, nineteenth-century cash-crop commercialisation and twentieth-century public health initiatives drove unprecedented demographic expansion that shaped the modern geography of the archipelago.
